=== FILE: Are You Low T？ How Lab Tests Diagnose Testosterone Issues [HyvypvrkHTs].en.txt ===

Let's talk about the testosterone lab ranges and how it's used to diagnose people. Historically speaking, people are diagnosed with low testosterone based on the parameters of falling outside of what a normal lab range is. A low testosterone diagnosis is pretty much a statistical diagnosis. When creating reference intervals, lab companies, what they do is they take aggregates of data. They get averages from hundreds of people to thousands of people. I've seen some studies in which some labs can use as little as a couple hundred people and I've seen some studies where they use more and what they do they get an aggregation of data and they keep the middle 95% of people. So what they do is if they have 2.5% of the outliers on the top are shaved off then 2.5% of the outliers on the bottom are shaved off and what you find in the middle the middle 95% is what they keep. I've also seen where they'll only shave off the top 5%. Or they'll only shave off the bottom 5%. But typically, it's usually they keep the middle 95%. One of the big problems about this is the fact that this is a statistical diagnosis. If the lab ranges would corroborate the blood levels with the patient's symptomology, it would provide us something more tangible. It provide us more of a qualitative uh diagnosis. But right now, it's pretty much just statistical diagnosis, meaning you fall inside the reference or you don't. We see a lot of guys who will fall well inside the reference range who do complain about all the symptoms of low testosterone. And by having a statistical diagnosis only, there's probably thousands of men who are walking around with all the symptoms, but they're completely being overlooked. A big thing we really have to take into consideration is what we determine as healthy. Because the term healthy is well quite frankly it's a relative term. So even if you use people in the decision-m of creating reference intervals who are otherwise deemed healthy, it doesn't necessarily mean they're free of some kind of evolving underlying diagnosis. Doesn't mean they have the absence of a subclinical thing going on. But the thing I really want to dial home is that especially in terms of the HRT world, in terms of our testosterone levels, is that if the reference interval does reflect a a quote unquote healthy population, but this healthy population lives the American d lives the American lifestyle in which, you know, they're eating a poor diet. They're not exercising, not getting adequate sunlight, not getting adequate sleep. They're working 40, 60 hours a week. completely sedentary and they're completely just showered in fluorescent lights. If that is what constitutes a healthy reference range and a healthy hormone level, then are they actually truly healthy or are we just accepting the fact that there's been been a massive decline in what a healthy hormone level should actually be? Long story short, when it comes to lab ranges, especially within the HRT, the TRT world, the lab ranges don't really tell us a whole lot. It really doesn't give us the full clinical picture, the full story. The big thing is how are you responded? How is the therapy treating you in terms of symptomatic improvement? Are you having improvements in body composition and overall well-being? Those are really the big driving factors and the the big clinical benchmarks in terms of how you're responding to the treatment. So, no, we're really not number driven, nor are we chasing a specific number. So if someone is saying you need to be a certain number, the therapy needs to get you to right here or only right here, that overlooks the symptomatic clinical outcomes that therapy is really being driven by.

What is TRT or Testosterone Replacement Therapy? TRT is an acronym for testosterone replacement therapy or testosterone substitution therapy often referred to as hormone therapy or androgen replacement therapy. TRT is a medical treatment used to treat low testosterone levels that occur with age or as a result of a medical condition. A man's body naturally produces less testosterone as he ages. This is a normal physiological process that occurs in his late 20s or early 30s. This gradual decline in testosterone levels most often does not produce noticeable symptoms, but as the years go by, the following symptoms may occur: erectile dysfunction, low libido, less frequent spontaneous erections or reduced sperm volume, sleep problems, loss of muscle mass and bone density, and unexplained weight gain. The only way to truly know if we have low testosterone levels is to have our blood levels checked along with other parameters, which are explained in several videos on this YouTube channel. === FILE: Hormones and Skin - How Hormone Optimization Therapy can benefit skin quality [M4D6w6DVKOU].en.txt ===

In this video about Hormones and Skin we will discuss How Hormone Optimization Therapy can benefit skin quality. Please like and subscribe. Thank you! And hit that notification bell so you won’t miss anything. Hormones are intrinsically involved with processes affecting the maintenance of skin health, such as collagen content, skin lipid levels, elasticity, wound healing, glycosaminoglycan content, and facial hair patterns. A major culprit for the skin thinning, wrinkling, and dryness associated with aging is the decline in hormones such as estrogen and progesterone in women, and testosterone in men.\h Therefore, it's\hno coincidence that the decline in hormone levels as people age parallels the decline in skin properties frequently associated with aging. There are four hormones that have the most profound effect on skin and health as you age. These are estrogen, testosterone, thyroid hormones, and cortisol. As we age, estrogen levels decline, creating significant changes in how the skin looks and feels. Specifically, skin becomes dry, less elastic, and more fragile. For women over the age of 40, declining estrogen levels is the leading cause of dry, sagging skin. Estrogen appears to aid in the prevention of skin aging in several ways. This reproductive hormone prevents a decrease in skin collagen in postmenopausal women; topical and systemic estrogen therapy can increase the skin collagen content and therefore maintain skin thickness. In addition, estrogen maintains skin moisture by increasing acid mucopolysaccharides and hyaluronic acid in the skin and possibly maintaining stratum corneum barrier function. Obese men and women often don’t show this deterioration in skin health to the same extent as normal weight people; this is because they maintain higher estrogen levels as a result of increased aromatase activity in fat and skin tissue. Studies of estrogen replacement therapy have shown some improvement in those skin properties affected by low estrogen levels, e.g. increased collagen content, skin thickness, and skin elasticity. Another important hormone involved in skin health is testosterone. Testosterone stimulates the sebum-producing glands, which are important for protecting skin with natural oils, but overproduction can lead to acne. Testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone are hormones needed to help your body maintain the delicate balance known as homeostasis. Age-related hormonal changes, such as experienced during puberty and menopause, may cause shifts in testosterone and metabolism. This can make your skin more oily or prone to breakouts. Low testosterone in men is associated with thinning skin. This is thought to be because there is less testosterone available for local conversion to estrogen through the action of aromatase present in the skin. Testosterone replacement has been found to increase skin thickness. Progesterone has been used in cosmetic skin creams as well as in hormone replacement therapy, and has been found to improve skin thickness and elasticity. Low progesterone levels are thought to increase the impact of androgens on sebaceous glands and body and head hair. This is because progesterone reduces 5-alpha reductase activity, which converts testosterone to its active metabolite dihydrotestosterone (DHT). DHT is the culprit for androgenic side effects in women such as unwanted facial hair growth, which tends to appear with aging. In both men and women, excess DHT in the skin contributes to acne, and in the skin of the scalp it is responsible for “male pattern baldness.” High levels of hormones can contribute to skin discoloration, the brown patches (“chloasma”) associated with pregnancy or with hormone replacement therapy. Thyroid is another hormone that influences your skin’s appearance. An overactive thyroid can cause warm, sweaty, and flushed skin, while an under-active thyroid can lead to dry, coarse skin with a reduced ability to perspire. Cortisol is your stress hormone. Your adrenal glands release cortisol and surges of this hormone may cause increased sebum production, an acne trigger. Excess cortisol also amps up inflammation, which can make almost any skin condition worse, including acne, eczema, rosacea, and vitiligo. Chronically high levels of cortisol also lead to sugar cravings, and we know that excess sugar increases both skinflammation and breakouts. High insulin levels (often from eating too much sugar or high glycemic index foods) have been shown to stimulate sebum production and androgen activity, which leads to acne. Clearly, human growth hormone (HGH) is a key player in the health and aging of our skin, and more and more research shows just how vital HGH is to helping us both feel and look younger. Human growth hormone is quickly rising to the forefront of the "anti-aging" world. Prescription growth hormone injections are extremely expensive, and the research into oral compounds capable of increasing mean, endogenous, bioactive, serum growth hormone levels is still preliminary. But I’m sure we’ll hear much more about all this in the very near future. To conclude: While hormone optimization therapy is not usually recommended solely for cosmetic purposes, it may have the added benefit of improving skin wellness and thereby saving substantial costs in cosmetic treatments. === FILE: How To Open Ampoule Right Way [kvO1UIq-AOA].en.txt ===

How To Open Ampoule Right Way safely and without getting glass in your fingers? In this demonstration video, I open a glass ampoule of Testosterone 250, which is an example of a Testosterone enanthate, one of the most common testosterones used in Testosterone Replacement Therapy. But of course, this technique can be used for whatever glass ampule you want to open. And if this is your first time here, make sure to subscribe so you can learn more about fitness and nutrition, hormones and anti-aging, all this to optimize your life overall. And hit that notification bell so you won’t miss anything. Okay, let’s start by stating the obvious: first wash your hands thoroughly and use some kind of sanitiser gel. Then Make sure all the oil is in the bottom part of the ampoule before opening it. You can gently tap with your finger to get it down if necessary. First take a closer look at the glass ampoule. The point where the ampoule will break is at the smallest part, called the neck. You will also note a black dot. This is the pressure point. To open the ampoule, hold it with both hands. Use your left hand to support the lower part of the ampoule or base part, and the right hand underneath the upper part. Make sure the black dot is pointed towards you, and both thumbs are on top of the glass ampoule. Both your index fingers will be under the ampoule. This is the starting position. Now to actually break the ampoule, you will have to put pressure on it, by squeezing your index fingers closer together, and by moving your thumbs away from each other, so the ampoule will break towards you. Avoid any pushing, pulling, or twisting actions while applying pressure on the ampoule to open it. Because I realize, if this is your first time you want to open this kind of glass ampoule, you probably going to wanna watch several times. That’s why I will go over this once again. Pick up the ampoule and hold its lower part between your thumb and index finger. Make sure to remove all the liquid from the top of the ampoule by gently tapping it with a finger of the other hand. Hold the ampoule so that the colored dot faces you. Grasp the top of the ampoule with your other hand. Place your thumb onto the colored dot and the index finger on the opposite side of the bulbous part of the ampoule. Hold the bottom of the ampoule firmly in an upright position and push the top section away from the colored dot with light, even pressure. The ampoule should break with a clean snap. Using too much force can cause the ampoule to shatter! If the ampoule shatters, discard it and use a new ampoule. If the ampoule does not break open, readjust its position in your hands and try again. If it seems extremely hard to open, do not try to open it by force. Try with a different ampoule first. Congratulations, you opened the ampule. Now put the bottom half down and discard the top. Your medication is now ready to be drawn from the ampule and to be used as directed by your physician.

However, if any doubt, go find yourself a medical doctor that can help you out. This is only general advise, and without studying the skin up close, it is impossible to give any personalized advice. It is very important to make a distinction between an infection and purely inflammation and pain. Signs of infection are -next to redness, swelling and pain- systemic reactions like fever and/or the presence of pus at the injection site. This can be under the form of a pustule or an abscess. In case of an infection, you really need to go see a doctor to get a prescription of local and/or systemic antibiotics. Sometimes an abscess needs to be drained by a doctor. If there is only inflammation, under the form of redness, swelling, pain, and the feeling of a hard subcutaneous nodule or lump, then the following actions can be taken. You can be conservative, and just wait it out. As said before, in most cases the reactions will be temporary. The inflammation reaches its maximum after one to two days, and then slowly fades down. The whole process can take up to 2 weeks. Sometimes a painless subcutaneous lump can still be palpitated months after the injection. Next, cold is recommended in the first 48hours of appearance of the skin reaction. It is especially helpful to reduce swelling and control pain. Ice is most effective when it is applied early and often for the first 48 hours. Local application of creams, containing anti-inflammatory cortisone can be very helpful. Check out the video in this card if you want to learn more about the different kinds of cortison cream and which type is best for this very purpose. Systemically, an over the counter antihistamine drug, like for example Cetirizine or Loratadine, can help with the swelling, a painkiller type paracetamol or aspirin (if you’re not allergic to it) can of course help with the pain, and a Non Steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, like for example diclofenac or ibuprofen, can be useful to fight the pain, the swelling and the redness. Remember these drugs are more than just pain relievers. They also help to reduce the inflammation and they lower fevers. Some subcutaneous nodules or lumps can remain for several weeks, and sometimes even months. They are mostly seen when doing subcutaneous injections or when there is a leakage out of the muscle after doing an intra-muscular injection. These lumps do not require any treatment once the pain is gone. They gradually will decrease. You know, I made another video about this, go and click on this thumbnail to watch it right now. Corticosteroid medicines are derivatives of the natural corticosteroid hormones that are produced by the adrenal glands. These have many important functions in the body, including control of inflammatory responses. Corticosteroid medicines are mainly used for their effect in controlling inflammation, and topical corticosteroids are applied directly to your skin (as opposed to taking a pill by mouth) to provide relief for a wide variety of dermatological conditions. They can also be used as a relief for post injection pain and reactions, if these are not infected, as I have explained in previous videos, that I will link under this one. Topical corticosteroids can be prescribed or purchased over-the-counter, depending on their strength. Corticosteroids are often simply called steroids, but it should be noted that they are very different from another group of steroids, for example anabolic steroids. Topical steroids are absorbed into the skin cells. They stop these cells from producing various inflammation-causing chemicals that are normally released when the skin reacts to allergens or irritation. These inflammation-causing chemicals include prostaglandins and various other inflammatory substances. They cause blood vessels to widen and other inflammatory substances to arrive, resulting in the affected area of skin becoming red, swollen and itchy. By preventing these inflammatory chemicals from being released in the skin, corticosteroids reduce inflammation and relieve its related symptoms such as itchiness. They can come in different forms\hincluding: Creams, the form that's prescribed most often, are a mixture of water and oils\hand usually contains a preservative. They're especially good for hairy and wet areas and are easily applied without a greasy feel. Ointments\hare made of oils and little to no water\hand don't usually contain a preservative. They're great for dry, scaly skin or areas with thick skin like the soles of your feet and the palms of your hands. Gels are made with water and propylene glycol and, like creams, they're easy to apply. Solutions, foams, and lotions\husually contain oil, water, and other chemicals and are used on your scalp. Topical steroids can be divided into four different strengths – mild, moderate, potent and very potent. The strength of a topical steroid is determined by a standardized test that measures the extent to which it can cause your blood vessels to constrict in the upper dermis (the layer of skin that's just below the outer epidermis). Comparatively speaking, a very potent topical steroid is between 600 and 1,000 times stronger than a mild one. The mildest one is Hydrocortisone 1%. Of course there are different brand names. Very often this strength can be bought over-the-counter. Moderate strength cortisone creams are Triamcinolone acetonide 0.1%, Fluocinolone acetonide 0.025%, and Mometasone furoate 0.1%. Potent strength topical corticosteroids include dipropionate 0.05%, Betamethasone dipropionate 0.05%, and Betamethasone valerate 0.1%. Very potent strength topical corticosteroids include Clobetasol propionate 0.05%, and Betamethasone\hdipropionate\h0.25%. Okay, now to the practical side of things. To get relief of inflammatory post-injection reactions such as pain, swelling and redness, a potent or even very potent strength topical corticosteroid can be used. There is no need to worry about frequently mentioned side-effects such as skin thinning (atrophy), enlarged blood vessels (telangiectasia) and Stretch marks (striae), since all these are really only seen on prolonged use of unnecessarily potent topical steroids, and not at all if you use them as indicated for inflammatory post-injection reactions. The general recommendations are using this potent to very potent strength topical corticosteroid for 3 to 5 days maximum, and massage the cream on the affected area twice or three times a day. Liver thyroid relationship, that is today's topic. The reason why I'm talking about this today is because statistically speaking about 30% of people who have some kind of underlying liver disease, liver dysfunction, may also have a correlating or accompanying thyroid dysfunction as well. Now, the literature in the last 10, 15-ish years is starting to elucidate that having liver disease in a lot of cases is and can be a type of hypothyroidism. And we've started calling this term called liver hypothyroidism. It's also referred to as intrahepatic hypothyroidism as well. So, pathophysiologically, this makes a lot of sense because if you remember about 80 80% of the T4 to T3 conversion, this this occurs peripherally, meaning not within the thyroid, but somewhere else um distal to the thyroid. Now, of that 80% T4 to T3 conversion, almost 60% of that occurs within the liver itself. So, even if your hypothalamus to thyroid axis is working well, or even the thyroid itself is very healthy, is very robust, is working well, the fact that upwards of 60% of your T4 to T3 conversion occurs in the liver tells us that a lot of your thyroid hormone is contingent on having a healthy liver. Now, consider the overwhelming prevalence of the the umbrella, the spectrum of metabolic diseases that exist in our Western populations, or should I say almost worldwide now. So, under that umbrella, we're talking about obesity, we're talking about mash, m a s h, which is formerly known as nash. Think about diabetes, insulin resistance, all of that, metabolic syndrome. All those things fall under this spectrum. Now, anything in that spectrum can be a possible contributor to having what's known as liver hypothyroidism and/or intrahepatic hypothyroidism. Now, just think about the overall prevalence of that spectrum of metabolic diseases I just mentioned, those are all the target populations who may be susceptible to having this condition. From a diagnostic standpoint, things may get a little tricky here. First of all, TSH is not a good marker for identifying this condition. TSH may be normal, it may be low-ish normal. Now, T4 on the other hand, it might be normal, or sometimes it may be a little bit on the higher end of normal, which I find somewhat interesting. Now, this is most likely due to the pituitary's upregulation of deiodinase 2. Now, there's and that's a compensatory mechanism. Now, there's D1, D2, D3. Now, principally, in states of low thyroid activity or underactive um thyroid conversion, deiodinase 2 tends to get upregulated as a compensatory mechanism because the brain says, "Hey, I don't detect enough T3, so what I'm going to do is I'm going to try to increase my activity so I can provide more raw material in hopes that you'll produce more T3 from the raw material." And in this this case, the raw material is the T4. And this makes sense because if you provide more T4, which in this case would be the raw material in the context of upregulating deiodinase 2, the goal is to increase conversion of that T4 to T3. So, obviously, T3 levels are expected to be typically rather low, and this would meet the criteria for euthyroid sick syndrome, which essentially means you have low low T3 in the context of normal TSH and/or T4. Additionally, since this is a state of chronic stress, which is the liver's being chronically stressed due to metabolic diseases, the D3 enzyme activity would be expected to be upregulated. So, thus, your RT3 would be expected to be elevated as well. So, here's the take-home message. If you have poor tolerance of thyroid meds, there's a chance maybe you have some underlying liver disease, liver dysfunction that might be going on. Or if you have anything under the constellation of metabolic diseases, again, obesity, diabetes, insulin resistance, mash, fatty liver, whatever you want to call it. If you drink alcohol pretty regularly, then chances are you may have intrahepatic hypothyroidism at least to some degree. And no, taking a ton of liver supplements isn't going to magically improve your liver and thus your thyroid. Instead, you're going to have to work on treating the underlying issue, which is the metabolic disease itself.

=== FILE: Qu'est-ce que la Thérapie de Remplacement de la Testostérone TRT？ (FRENCH FRANÇAIS) [u753lI96p40].en.txt ===

PRT is the acronym for testosterone replacement therapy, sometimes called hormone therapy or testosterone replacement therapy. It's a medical treatment used to treat low testosterone levels, which can occur with age or due to a medical condition. Your body naturally produces less testosterone as you age; this is a completely natural process that begins in your late twenties or early thirties. This gradual decrease in testosterone often doesn't cause any noticeable symptoms, but after a few years, the following symptoms may occur: decreased libido, fewer spontaneous erections, erectile dysfunction, decreased sperm count or volume, sleep problems, unusual muscle and bone loss, and unexplained weight gain. The only way to know if you truly have low testosterone levels is to have your blood levels checked, along with a few other things that are explained on this channel, including several other videos. There are several ways to administer testosterone: gels, injections, creams, patches, nasal spray, oral medications, and implants.  But almost all the experts who have appeared on this channel agree that the best methods are injections or custom-made testosterone cream for daily application to the scrotum. You can learn much more about this in other videos we 've made previously. TRT is generally lifelong because it replaces your own insufficient testosterone production with exogenous testosterone. If you stop TRT, you revert to your own insufficient testosterone production, so all the symptoms will return. Watch other videos we've made on the possible side effects and costs of TRT—two common questions, but the most important one is this: before starting TRT, make sure you learn as much as possible about it. Find a good provider who can help you on your journey to better health and a better quality of life. To help you in these two areas, I created the Facebook group " TLTI and Hormones Optimization." Many of the experts you see in videos on this channel are part of this Facebook group and can help you find a good clinic and answer any questions you may have. Now do this: click here to start our list  a reading that will teach you all the basics to start trp

=== FILE: Skin Changes on TRT and How to Fix it - by Dermatologist Dr. Steven Devos [8yfKrRmQNh8].en.txt ===

Embarking on testosterone replacement therapy can be a life-changing decision, offering benefits like increased energy, improved mood, and enhanced physical performance. However, as your body adjusts to new hormonal levels, you may notice unexpected changes in your skin, ranging from increased oiliness and acne to dryness or sensitivity. These shifts can feel frustrating, especially when they impact your confidence and comfort. These changes stem from testosterone's impact on sebaceous glands which ramp up sebum production and its conversion to dihydrotestosterone DHT a potent androgen that can affect hair follicles and skin. The first step in managing skin changes on TRT is recognizing what's happening. Testosterone increases sebum production which can clog pores and lead to acne especially on the face, chest, and back. Studies show that up to 70% of men on TRT may experience acne after 2 years with severity peaking in the first 6 to 12 months. Additionally, higher testosterone levels can elevate DHT, potentially triggering hair loss in those genetically predisposed. The first action step is to track your skin's response to TRT. Note when the acne breakouts occur, their severity, and any hair thinning. This helps you and your healthcare provider adjust your treatment if needed. Regular chickens with a dermatologist can provide professional insights into your skin's condition. To help you with this, I wrote an ebook, How a Man's Skin Changes on TRT and How to Fix It. As you know, I'm a dermatologist with over 20 years of experience, and I'm on TRT since 2017. Whether you are just starting TRT or navigating long-term effects, this ebook is your guide to understanding your skin's response and reclaiming a healthy, vibrant complexation. From skincare routines to lifestyle tweaks and expertbacked treatments, I'll empower you with the tools to look and feel your best on this transformative journey. But of course, I will share some information in this very video. A consistent skin care routine can counteract the increased oiliness and acne caused by TRT. The goal is to manage excess sebum without stripping your skin which can lead to irritation and more oil production. So wash your face twice daily with a gentle non-comdogenic cleanser to remove excess oil and prevent clogged pores. Avoid harsh soaps that can irritate your skin. Exfoliate one to two times a week to remove the dead skin cells that can clog pores. Use a product with salicylic acid which penetrate pores to reduce acne causing bacteria. Concerning moisturizing, apply an oil-free, lightweight moisturizer to keep your skin hydrated without adding to oiliness. Hydration helps regulate seum production and prevents your skin from overcompensating with more oil. For sun protection, use a non-comdogenic sunscreen daily as TRT can make your skin more sensitive to sun damage, which can worsen acne scars. In the description of this video, you will find a link to Mizumi Skincare, a brand I can recommend for all TRT and acne related skin problems. For some men, combining TRT with other treatments can help manage skin changes more effectively. So, for sebum control treatments, you can consider topical retinoids or medications that reduce oiliness. They can be used alongside TRT to control sebum production. Emerging research suggests that hono, a compound that modulates the testosterone pathway, may have anti-rinkle and skin densifying effects. While more studies are needed, honolulas based creams, could be a future option for improving skin texture on TRT. TRT offers transformative benefits for men seeking to reclaim their energy, strength, and overall well-being. However, this journey comes with skin challenges ranging from increased oiliness and acne to potential hair loss that can impact confidence and quality of life. These changes driven by hormonal shifts and elevated DHT levels are manageable with the right knowledge and strategies. Ultimately, TRT is more than just hormone optimization. It's about feeling your best inside and out. By applying some practical evidence-based strategies, you can overcome skin changes, prevent long-term damage, and embrace the full benefits of TRT with confidence. Are desiccated thyroid hormones going away? On August 6th, 2025, yes, just a few days ago, the FDA issued a letter to manufacturers, importers, and distributors of these desecated thyroid hormones that they will now need to pursue a biologics license in order to continue offering these products. In the letter, the FDA also referred to these desecated thyroid products as ADTS or animal derived thyroid products. If you aren't aware, it would affect drugs such as nature thyroid, NP thyroid, armor thyroid, nathyroid, as well as adisa or even compound versions of those. As of right now, it's speculated that there's somewhere in the ballpark of about 1 and a half to 2 million people who currently use these NDT products. Here's the big problem with this is that obtaining a biologics license is incredibly expensive, very cumbersome, and it is a lengthy process. Remember about five or six years ago when HCG became reclassified as a biologic and then numerous compoundies went from offering it to practically overnight pulling the plug on it. Now HCG is incredibly hard to obtain from a compounding pharmacy. You for most people they have to go the name brand route. Well, this could also happen to these thyroid medications and that would increase the difficulty of accessibility to these medications. As of right now, it does not appear the FDA is taking action against any of these manufacturers or distributors. But per the letter, it does appear that there's about a one-year grace period so that patients can get converted transitioned over to the other traditional products such as levothyoxine or liioyronine. What is TAT ​​or Testosterone Replacement Therapy? TAT is an acronym for Testosterone Replacement Therapy, sometimes also called Hormone or Androgen Replacement Therapy. It is a medical treatment to treat low testosterone levels, which can occur due to age or as a result of illness. The body produces less testosterone as we age; this is a completely natural process that begins in our late 20s or early 30s. This gradual reduction in production usually causes no symptoms, but after a few years, the following symptoms may appear: decreased libido, less frequent spontaneous erections, erectile dysfunction, low sperm count, sleep problems, unusual loss of muscle and bone density, loss of energy, and unexplained weight gain. To find out if you really have low testosterone, the only way is to have your blood levels checked, along with some other things that are explained in several videos on this channel. What we've done so far is that testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) is usually a lifelong decision, as it replaces the body's own insufficient testosterone production with exogenous testosterone. If someone stops the TRT, the original symptoms return because the body reverts to its original insufficient testosterone production. === FILE: Why Your IGF-1 Test Might Be LYING About Growth Hormone - The Surprising Truth [YH1UDMWKvA0].en.txt ===

Let's talk about the problems with IGF-1 testing. Now, IGF-1 is the downstream surrogate biomarker of growth hormone production. So, for a quick lesson, the hypothalamus makes growth hormone releasing hormone that tells the anterior pituitary, make growth hormone. And therefore, that has a downstream signal telling the liver to make IGF-1. And roughly about 70 75ish% of total IGF-1 production comes from the liver. Now you would think, okay, cool. So this would be a good surrogate marker to to see at least what is 75% of my body's total IGF-1 production, right? That's what we would think. But measuring IGF-1 really isn't inherently that clinically significant. It really does not carry a lot of specificity in terms of who does not have adult growth hormone deficiency. And here's why. There's several problems with IGF-1 testing. Yes, it can be used to try to roll in rule out who might have adult growth hormone deficiency, but we know that the diagnostic sensitivity of IGF-1 testing as you get older, as you start approaching 35, 40-ish, it really starts to lose its sensitivity. Now what the literature has shown us is that in puberty age, adolescent age, yeah, it it is more sensitivity as to who does and who does not have low IGF-1. But as you get older, particularly 3540ish, there appears to be an overlap between who has adult growth hormone deficiency and who doesn't have adult growth hormone deficiency. In other words, the sensitivity is lost as you get older. Another thing to think about is that there are clinical cases in which GH levels can be normal, but low IGF-1 may be present. Some people refer to this as quote unquote hpatic resistance. In other words, the brain is telling the liver to make IGF-1, but the liver is not making it in response to that GH release. Some of these conditions could be liver disease. Let's say MASH or MASH, which means metabolic associated stato hepatitis. Now, that's formerly known as fatty liver disease or NFLD, whatever you want to refer to it as. Other conditions that can lead to low IGF-1 in the presence of normal GH, hypothyroidism, that one's somewhat common to be honest with you. Yes, the thyroid hormones are involved in the production of IGF-1 from the liver. Low calorie diets, chronic dieting, malnutrition, anorexia, things like that. If you're in a chronically dieting type phase, that too can lead to a reduction, a downplay in the production of IGF-1 from the liver. Big one, obesity. We know that probably about 30% of the country right now is obese. Diabetes, insulin resistance, those are other big players in the western countries that also inhibits IGF-1 release. Yeah, they'll still make it, but it does blunt how much they can make. Now, we know sex hormones plays a role as well. Yes. So hypogonatism is another big player in the production of IGF-1. So in my opinion, the big levers you want to pull if you want to increase the production of IGF-1, if they got low tea, address it. If they're insulin resistant, obese, they need to address that. If they have hypothyroidism, treat it accordingly. Another one that I didn't mention yet is that sleep apnea is another big player. And that's because growth hormone is robustly primarily made in pulsatile fashion during deep wave sleep. And if you have sleep apnnea, you are disrupting that sleep pattern. You're not hitting those deep wave sleep that you're going to need to produce GH and thus IGF-1. And another cause would be what referred to as iatrogenic, meaning medical intervention causes it. That would be the introduction of aromatase inhibitors. So as I just mentioned, hypogonatism can cause low IGF-1 in the context of normal GH. But if you get them on TRT, that should bring that production up. But then if you introduce aromatase inhibitors, you're kind of just negating that possible benefit because you're blocking estrogen. And we know that estradile is a big lever that stimulates the production of IGF-1. And these are just a few reasons why drawing IGF-1 levels aren't exactly the most specific and sensitive towards who may and who may not have low growth hormone production.

=== FILE: ¿Qué es TRT o Terapia de Reemplazo de Testosterona？ (SPANISH ESPAÑOL) [dokcvJ3vnpc].en.txt ===

What is TRT or testosterone replacement therapy? TRT is the acronym for testosterone replacement therapy, sometimes called hormone replacement therapy or androgen replacement therapy. It is a medical treatment used to treat low testosterone levels that can occur with age or as a result of a medical condition. Your body naturally produces less testosterone as you age; it is a completely natural process that begins in your late 20s or early 30s. This gradual decline in testosterone often doesn't cause any noticeable symptoms, but after a few years, the following symptoms may occur: low libido, fewer spontaneous erections, erectile dysfunction, decreased sperm count and volume, sleep problems, unusual loss of muscle mass and bone density, and unexplained weight gain. The only way to know if you truly have low testosterone levels is to have your levels checked in the blood, along with some other things explained on this channel in several other videos. There are several ways to administer testosterone: gels, injections, creams, patches, nasal spray, oral medications, and pellets. But almost all the experts who have appeared on this channel agree that the best ways are injections or testosterone compound cream for daily use. In the scrotum, you can learn much more about this in other videos we've made previously. TRT is generally lifelong, as it replaces insufficient testosterone production with exogenous testosterone. If TRT is stopped, you will return to your own insufficient testosterone production, and all the symptoms will return. Look for other videos we 've made about the possible side effects and the cost of TRT, which are common questions. But the bottom line is this: before starting TRT, make sure you learn as much as possible about it and find a good provider who can help you on your journey to better health and quality of life. To help you with both, I've created the RT and Hormone Optimization Facebook group. Many experts you see in the videos on this channel are in this Facebook group and can help you find a good clinic and answer any questions you may have. Now do this: Click here to start our playlist that will teach you all the basics about how to start TRT.
